content: In all studies, the implementation of a central line-associated bloodstream infection (CLABSI) care bundle was accompanied by additional measures such as targeted training, supportive materials, organizational culture change, executive support, surveillance, and promotional campaign materials like posters. However, one study evaluating a statewide surgical site infection (SSI) multimodal strategy found no improvement in surgical outcomes during the study period. Three studies demonstrated a significant reduction in infection rates following the introduction of a CLABSI care bundle focused on insertion and maintenance practices in pediatric ICUs. Another study reported a decrease in MRSA SSI rates during the intervention period for orthopedic and cardiac surgeries. A collaborative quality improvement strategy in neonatal ICUs in the USA, targeting CLABSI prevention through care bundles and training, was associated with a significant reduction in healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) after risk adjustment. A statewide multimodal program aimed at reducing catheter-related bloodstream infections and ventilator-associated pneumonia through care bundles, cultural change, training, teamwork, and communication showed reductions in mortality at one and two years post-implementation, though no significant difference in adjusted length of stay was observed. Two studies on national multimodal infection prevention and control (IPC) programs to reduce MRSA infections showed a decline in MRSA colonization or infection rates with interventions such as MRSA screening, culture change, training, and funding. A significant downward trend in MRSA bacteremia rates was linked to a national IPC program that included alcohol-based hand rubs, performance feedback, campaign materials, and policy reviews. National multimodal hand hygiene programs yielded mixed results. In one Australian study, compliance and HAI rates were measured after a statewide hand hygiene campaign, showing significant impacts on two out of four clinical MRSA indicators, though other IPC interventions may have influenced these results. Another national hand hygiene program using targeted training, alcohol-based hand rubs, and performance feedback showed an estimated average improvement in hand hygiene compliance in intervention hospitals compared to controls. The GDG (Guideline Development Group) considered the overall quality of evidence to be low due to medium to high risk of bias across studies. However, they strongly recommended the interventions, emphasizing their importance in improving practices and reducing HAIs and antimicrobial resistance (AMR). All studies were conducted in high-income countries, limiting generalizability to other settings. Non-EPOC studies, including 48 additional studies, supported implementing national IPC activities using multimodal strategies and care bundles, though they were excluded from the main analysis due to study design limitations. Five studies demonstrated that multimodal strategies improved hand hygiene compliance. Care bundles, whether standalone or part of multimodal strategies, were associated with reduced rates of ventilator-associated pneumonia, CLABSI, SSI, catheter-related bloodstream infections, bloodstream infections, and catheter-associated urinary tract infections. When combined with broader safety programs, including checklists, education tools, and teamwork promotion, reductions in central-line days and CLABSI rates were observed. One study linked a hand hygiene initiative with education and feedback across six states to decreased bloodstream infection rates in four states. Four studies associated reductions in MRSA transmission and infections with quality improvement programs, national IPC programs, and campaigns like Clean Your Hands. A carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae prevention program was associated with decreased prevalence and improved IPC compliance. A downward trend in Clostridioides difficile incidence was observed with standardized clinical infection prevention and environmental cleaning protocols. The GDG emphasized the importance of regular monitoring, auditing, and feedback of IPC practices to prevent and control HAIs and AMR. Feedback should be provided to all audited individuals and relevant staff, including hospital management and senior administration, to drive both individual and organizational change. IPC teams and committees should be involved, as IPC practices are quality markers for these programs. Monitoring and feedback aim to engage stakeholders, create partnerships, and develop working groups and networks. The GDG also highlighted the need for periodic evaluation of IPC programs to assess goal achievement, identify gaps, and improve practices. Evaluation should be based on documented outcomes, including compliance with IPC practices, process indicators, and resource allocation. The auditing process should be conducted in a blame-free manner to promote a non-punitive institutional culture. Communication and sharing of results are critical to the process. The GDG acknowledged the challenges of implementing these recommendations in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs) due to resource constraints but suggested partnerships and collaborations, such as the WHO African Partnerships for Patient Safety model, to support program delivery and funding. Cost-effectiveness studies showed that quality improvement programs could lead to significant savings by reducing infection cases and associated costs. In conclusion, the GDG recognized the low quality of evidence but strongly recommended implementing national IPC programs with multimodal strategies to improve practices and reduce HAIs and AMR. They emphasized the importance of national-level support and coordination within the context of broader quality improvement agendas. Further research is needed to facilitate sustainable implementation, understand the impact of culture and context, and evaluate cost-effectiveness and outcomes.
